First, we can simplify the limit using trigonometric identities, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{\theta \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta } & ={lim}_{\theta \to 0}(\theta \operatorname{sec}⁡\theta ÷\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta ) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to 0}(\frac{\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }÷\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to 0}(\frac{\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }) \\  & ={lim}_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that as $\theta \to 0,$ both numerator and denominator approach $0.$

So, if we attempt to evaluate the limit directly, we get

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }=\frac{0}{0},
$$

which is an indeterminate form.

Instead, let's recall the following special limit:

$$
{lim}_{\theta \to 0}\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\theta }=1
$$

Rewriting the given limit using the algebra of limits and applying our special limit, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } & ={lim}_{\theta \to 0}{(\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\theta })}^{-1} \\  & ={[{lim}_{\theta \to 0}\,\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\theta }]}^{-1} \\  & ={1}^{-1} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$
